readings.unit: Complete JEP 444, Virtual Threads
readings.revision: JEP 444; official OpenJDK page; published Thu, 04 Jun 2026 17:38:09 GMT (Jina header timestamp, not verified as original publication date); retrieved 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: All 435 lines (1-435); Summary, History, Goals, Non-Goals, Motivation (4 subsections), Description including all Detailed changes (9 API areas), Alternatives, Testing, Risks and Assumptions, Dependencies; both code examples; one linked thread-dump screenshot was not rendered or inspected

sections: Motivation > Improving scalability with the asynchronous style
Motivation > Preserving the thread-per-request style with virtual threads
Description > Using virtual threads vs. platform threads
Description > Do not pool virtual threads
Description > Memory use and interaction with garbage collection
Detailed changes > Debugging (JVM TI, JDWP, JDI)
notes: Source claim: the three goals are throughput for thread-per-request servers at near-optimal hardware use, adoption through the existing java.lang.Thread API with minimal change, and troubleshooting with existing JDK tools; the non-goals explicitly exclude removing platform threads, changing Java's concurrency model, and adding a data-parallelism construct.

Source claim: the definition is contrastive - a virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread not tied to one OS thread, scheduled M:N onto carriers, versus platform threads (1:1) and early Java green threads (M:1); the scheduler is a work-stealing ForkJoinPool in FIFO mode whose parallelism defaults to availableProcessors and which is distinct from the LIFO common pool.

Source claim: most JDK blocking operations unmount the virtual thread; a few (notably filesystem operations and Object.wait) block the carrier, and their implementations temporarily expand scheduler parallelism up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize. Pinning, by contrast, is explicitly not compensated by parallelism expansion.

Source claim: JDK 21 pinning has exactly two stated causes - executing inside a synchronized block or method, or executing a native method or foreign function - and the JEP states pinning threatens scalability, not correctness.

Source claim: migration diagnostics are three distinct mechanisms - the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event (enabled by default, 20ms threshold), jdk.tracePinnedThreads with full/short modes, and jdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals for thread-local removal.

Source claim: the compatibility surface is wider than pinning - Thread.getAllStackTraces() is narrowed to platform threads, blocking Socket/ServerSocket/DatagramSocket I/O becomes interruptible (interrupt unparks and closes the socket), setDaemon and setPriority become no-ops, getThreadGroup returns a placeholder VirtualThreads group, SecurityManager gives no permissions, ThreadMXBean stays platform-only, and JVM TI GetAllThreads/GetAllStackTraces exclude virtual threads.

Source claim: the source and binary risks are enumerated narrowly - new Thread methods and the nested Thread.Builder interface can break subclasses at compile time, and the new final isVirtual() can raise IncompatibleClassChangeError if a compiled subclass declares a same-signature method.

Source claim: stacks live in the heap as growable stack-chunk objects, are not GC roots, and G1 does not support humongous stack chunks, so a stack reaching half a region (possibly as small as 512KB) may throw StackOverflowError - a per-thread stack limit, not a thread-count limit.

Source claim: observability is deliberately split rather than extended - jstack-style dumps are not widened to virtual threads; a new jcmd Thread.dump_to_file dump (text or JSON) groups threads, omits object addresses, locks, JNI and heap statistics, and does not pause the application; with jdk.trackAllThreads=false some builder-created threads may be absent from it.

Inference, not source claim: the illustrative figures (200 platform-pool tasks/s versus about 10,000 or 1,000,000 tasks/s) are presented as expected scale after warmup, with no measurement method or result table, so they must not be cited as benchmark evidence; likewise the 2026-06-04 header timestamp postdates the JDK 21 finalization the body describes and is best read as a page-served timestamp.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Its scope note says only named JEP 444 sections were inspected; this full-body read can now support the scheduler and pinning paragraphs from Scheduling virtual threads and Executing virtual threads, and the not-performed list can drop full JEP 491 body inspection once R016 is accepted.

The page treats pinning as the main release-dependent difference; the JEP adds behavioral differences that change migration advice independently - getAllStackTraces() narrowed to platform threads, blocking socket I/O becoming interruptible and closing the socket, setDaemon/setPriority no-ops, placeholder VirtualThreads group, and ThreadMXBean/JVM TI platform-only views.

The JEP separates two arguments that pooling advice often merges - virtual threads are too cheap to pool, and concurrency limits belong in constructs such as semaphores; check the page keeps no-pooling distinct from no-admission-control and leaves connection budgets to the connection-pool page.

Cancellation ownership can cite the JEP's stated side effect: interrupting a virtual thread blocked on Socket, ServerSocket or DatagramSocket unparks it and closes the socket, so interruption is not a neutral stop signal for a connection.

readings.revision: JEP 491; official OpenJDK page; no Published Time field present in the retrieved representation, so no publication date is asserted; retrieved 2026-10-24

sections: Motivation > Virtual threads are pinned in synchronized methods
Description > Diagnosing remaining cases of pinning
Description > The system property jdk.tracePinnedThreads is no longer needed
Description > Choosing between synchronized and java.util.concurrent.locks
notes: Source claim: the goal is that virtual threads blocking in synchronized methods and statements release their platform threads, so existing libraries that use synchronized need no rewrite to scale; a second goal is better diagnostics for the pinning that remains.

Source claim: the cause is bookkeeping, not language design - the JVM records monitor ownership against the carrier platform thread rather than the virtual thread, so unmounting inside a monitor would let the next virtual thread mounted on that carrier appear to own the monitor and destroy mutual exclusion, which is why the JVM prevents unmounting.

Source claim: three blocking shapes are addressed - blocking to enter a monitor held elsewhere, blocking inside a synchronized region, and Object.wait()/timed wait with monitor re-acquisition after notify; each now unmounts and is resubmitted to the scheduler, possibly resuming on a different carrier.

Source claim: the alternative of expanding scheduler parallelism is rejected on scaling grounds, since the maximum platform threads available to the scheduler is limited and stated to default to 256, so no parallelism value rescues many virtual threads blocked in monitors.

Source claim: diagnostics change in both directions - jdk.tracePinnedThreads is removed and setting it has no effect (it is also described as problematic because traces printed while executing critical code), while jdk.VirtualThreadPinned is retained for native/foreign callback pinning and enhanced to convey the pin reason and the carrier identity.

Source claim: remaining pinning is enumerated as exactly three Future Work cases - blocking while resolving a symbolic reference and loading a class, blocking inside a class initializer, and waiting for another thread to finish class initialization - each attributed to a native frame or blocking in the JVM, and described as rarely problematic.

Source claim: the only stated performance risk is narrow and directional - exiting a monitor may now have to queue a virtual thread to the scheduler, which is currently less efficient than unparking a platform thread; no throughput, latency or benchmark figure is given.

Source claim: the change depends on a Java 23 JVM TI specification change to GetObjectMonitorUsage so it no longer reports monitors owned by virtual threads, justified by the bookkeeping cost of locating monitors of unmounted virtual threads; the JEP body itself names no delivering JDK release for its own feature.

Inference, not source claim: the Summary's nearly all cases of pinning is deliberately scoped by native frames, the three Future Work cases and the retained event, so any statement that JDK 24 removes pinning would overstate the text; the defensible claim is that monitor-based pinning stops being a scheduler hazard in the covered cases.

Inference, not source claim: because the retrieved representation has no status or release header, the book's JDK 24 attribution cannot be confirmed from this file and must continue to rest on the release announcements already cited in the chapter; the 128-line body is also materially shorter than JEP 444 and omits testing and non-goal sections, which limits what compatibility evidence it can supply.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Lines 84, 100 and 134 rest on the implementation review and release announcements because the canonical body was not retrievable; R016 supplies that body, so the not-fully-accessible caveat can be retired and the unmount-while-holding-a-monitor mechanism sourced to Description, while the LM_LEGACY locking-mode caveat remains implementation-review-only and should be labelled as such.

The page carries jdk.tracePinnedThreads forward as a JDK 21 diagnostic; the JEP states the property is removed and that setting it has no effect, so any JDK 24+ guidance should state the release boundary and point to the retained jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event instead.

Replace a general some-pinning-remains hedge with the JEP's exact residual set - class loading and symbolic resolution, class initializer blocking, waiting for class initialization, and native/foreign callbacks - plus the narrow monitor-exit scheduling cost as the stated performance risk.

The case is a JDK 21 monitor-pinning incident; JEP 491 changes that specific cause but not instrumentation cost or downstream capacity, so the case should keep its JDK 21 vintage explicit and must not be read as describing current releases.

notes: Source claim: every cross-process call should have connection and request timeouts; too-high timeouts retain resources, too-low timeouts cause retries and can turn small latency increases into an outage.

Source claim: a practical timeout starts from the downstream latency distribution, for example accepting 0.1% false timeouts at p99.9, with padding for tight distributions and extra allowance for internet or connection setup.
Source claim: retries are selfish and can amplify overload; a five-layer stack with three retries per layer can multiply load by 243, so retrying at one layer is preferred for low-cost operations.
Source claim: exponential backoff should be capped, but a cap makes clients retry at a constant rate; limiting retry count and returning failure earlier is preferable.
Source claim: APIs with side effects need idempotency before retries are safe; client errors generally should not be retried, though eventual consistency blurs that boundary.
Source claim: jitter spreads correlated retries and periodic work; deterministic per-host jitter preserves reproducibility for diagnosis, while random jitter hides patterns.
Inference: the 0.1%/p99.9 choice is a policy trade-off, not a universal timeout formula; the article gives no adaptive control law.
Inference: the article is first-party operational guidance, not a controlled experiment; the 243x multiplication is arithmetic, not a measured incident.
